stem: The nurse assesses a sacral wound in a client who has been immobile since hip surgery. The wound bed shows full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat and some yellow slough, but the slough does not obscure the depth of tissue loss, and no bone, tendon, or muscle is exposed. Which stage of pressure injury should the nurse document, using current NPIAP staging terminology?
options: Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 4 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
rationale: A Stage 3 pressure injury involves full-thickness skin loss with visible adipose (fat) tissue; slough and/or eschar may be present but does not obscure the depth of tissue loss, and bone, tendon, and muscle are not exposed. Stage 2 involves only partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis (no fat visible). Stage 4 would show exposed bone, tendon, or muscle. Unstageable means slough or eschar obscures the wound bed so depth cannot be determined; here the depth is clearly visualized, so it is stageable as a Stage 3.
nursing_concept: NPIAP pressure injury staging

stem: A client with right knee osteoarthritis and mild right leg weakness is being taught to ambulate with a single-point cane. Which instruction should the nurse include?
options: Hold the cane in your right hand and advance the cane at the same time as your right leg
Hold the cane in your left hand and advance the cane at the same time as your right leg
Hold the cane in your right hand and advance the cane at the same time as your left leg
Hold the cane in your left hand and keep it stationary while both legs move together
rationale: A cane should be held in the hand on the stronger, unaffected side (the left hand, since the right leg is weak). This widens the base of support on the weaker side. The cane and the weaker (right) leg are advanced together, followed by the stronger (left) leg, which produces a smooth, supported gait. Holding the cane in the affected/right hand (A, C) removes the support advantage, and keeping the cane stationary (D) provides no assistance during the step.
nursing_concept: Cane use — correct hand and gait pattern

stem: A client receiving continuous enteral feeding through an NG tube has a witnessed coughing episode and reports feeling as though the tube shifted. The nurse checks the gastric residual volume and finds 400 mL, compared with 60 mL two hours earlier. The head of the bed is at 30 degrees. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Continue the feeding at the current rate and recheck the residual volume in 4 hours
Stop the feeding, keep the head of the bed elevated (or position the client laterally if distress is present), assess respiratory status, and notify the provider
Increase the feeding rate temporarily to flush the tubing before rechecking placement
Advance the tube 2 inches farther into the stomach and resume the feeding
rationale: Coughing, a sensation of tube displacement, and a large increase in residual volume are cues suggesting possible tube migration, delayed gastric emptying, and aspiration risk. The priority is to stop the feeding immediately, maintain a position that protects the airway (HOB elevated or side-lying if the client is in distress), assess respiratory status, and notify the provider before resuming. Continuing or increasing the rate (A, C) risks worsening aspiration, and blindly advancing the tube (D) without confirming placement is unsafe.
nursing_concept: Enteral feeding — aspiration risk recognition and response

stem: A nurse is monitoring a client receiving intermittent tube feedings for signs of aspiration. Which findings should the nurse recognize as indicating an increased risk for, or an occurring episode of, aspiration? Select all that apply.
options: Coughing or choking during or shortly after the feeding
Gastric residual volume significantly increased from the client's own baseline
New-onset drop in oxygen saturation with crackles heard on lung auscultation
The head of the bed remains elevated 30-45 degrees for 45 minutes after the feeding ends
Wet, gurgling vocal quality noted after the feeding
Bowel sounds are hypoactive in all four quadrants
rationale: Coughing/choking (A), a rising residual volume above the client's baseline (B), new hypoxemia with crackles (C), and a wet/gurgling voice (E) are all cues consistent with aspiration or high aspiration risk. Keeping the head of the bed elevated after a feeding (D) is a protective, recommended practice, not a warning sign. Hypoactive bowel sounds (F) reflect general GI motility and are not a specific aspiration indicator.
nursing_concept: Aspiration precautions with enteral feeding

stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an intermittent tube feeding through an established NG tube. Place the following actions in the correct order.
options: Check the gastric aspirate pH to help confirm the tube remains in the stomach
Elevate the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees
Compare the external tube length marking to the length documented at insertion
Perform hand hygiene and explain the procedure to the client
Begin administering the feeding at the prescribed rate
rationale: The nurse should first perform hand hygiene and explain the procedure to the client, then position the client with the head of the bed elevated at least 30 degrees to reduce aspiration risk, then check the external tube length against the documented insertion length as a quick displacement check, then aspirate and check gastric pH as an additional placement check, and only then begin the feeding. Checking placement before elevating the head of the bed or skipping the length/pH checks increases the risk of feeding a misplaced tube.
nursing_concept: NG tube feeding — placement verification sequence

stem: An older adult client on bedrest after surgery reports no bowel movement in 3 days and describes passing small, hard stools with straining when he last had one. Which intervention should the nurse recommend first to prevent fecal impaction?
options: Increase dietary fiber and fluid intake, and encourage mobility as tolerated
Administer a Fleet enema immediately without further assessment
Restrict oral fluids until a bowel movement occurs
Insert a rectal tube to stimulate peristalsis
rationale: For early, uncomplicated constipation, the least invasive and first-line measures are increasing fiber and fluid intake and promoting activity/mobility, which stimulate peristalsis. An enema (B) is more invasive and should not be the first step without further assessment (e.g., ruling out impaction requiring digital removal first). Restricting fluids (C) would worsen constipation. Rectal tubes (D) are not a standard constipation-prevention measure and carry risk of vagal stimulation/mucosal injury.
nursing_concept: Constipation prevention in the immobile client

stem: A nurse is teaching a client who will perform self-intermittent catheterization at home for a neurogenic bladder. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of the procedure?
options: "I will use a new catheter and full sterile technique every single time, even at home."
"I should catheterize on a regular schedule, such as every 4 to 6 hours, and whenever I feel bladder fullness."
"I only need to catheterize when I haven't urinated in over 24 hours."
"I should hold my urine as long as possible between catheterizations to help build bladder tone."
rationale: Intermittent self-catheterization at home is typically performed using clean (not sterile) technique on a regular schedule, generally every 4-6 hours, and additionally whenever the client senses fullness, to keep bladder volumes low and reduce UTI and overdistension risk. Requiring full sterile technique at home (A) is unnecessary and impractical. Waiting up to 24 hours (C) or deliberately holding urine (D) allows bladder overdistension, which increases infection risk and can damage the detrusor muscle.
nursing_concept: Intermittent catheterization — schedule and technique

stem: A client reports acute ankle pain, swelling, and bruising one hour after an inversion injury. Which nonpharmacological comfort measure should the nurse recommend at this time?
options: Apply a warm, moist compress to increase blood flow to the area
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel to the ankle for 15-20 minutes
Massage the ankle firmly to relieve muscle tension
Apply a heating pad set on high directly against the skin
rationale: In the first 24-48 hours after an acute musculoskeletal injury, cold application (wrapped to protect the skin, applied 15-20 minutes at a time) causes vasoconstriction that limits swelling and bleeding into tissue and helps numb pain. Heat (A, D) promotes vasodilation, which would worsen swelling in the acute phase, and applying it directly and on high risks a burn. Vigorous massage (C) over an acutely injured, swollen area can increase tissue damage and bleeding.
nursing_concept: Cold vs. heat application in acute injury

stem: A client reports difficulty falling asleep and frequent nighttime awakenings. Which teaching should the nurse include to promote healthy sleep hygiene?
options: "Exercise vigorously within an hour of bedtime to tire your body out."
"Use your bed only for sleep and intimacy; avoid working or watching TV in bed."
"Take a 2-hour nap in the late afternoon whenever you feel tired."
"Drink a glass of wine before bed to help you relax and fall asleep."
rationale: Reserving the bed only for sleep and intimacy strengthens the mental association between bed and sleep, a core sleep hygiene principle. Vigorous exercise close to bedtime (A) is stimulating and can delay sleep onset. Long or late afternoon naps (C) reduce the homeostatic drive to sleep at night. Alcohol (D) may cause initial drowsiness but fragments sleep and worsens nighttime awakenings, so it is not recommended as a sleep aid.
nursing_concept: Sleep hygiene principles

stem: A client who had a right-hemisphere stroke has left-sided hemiparesis and left unilateral neglect. During morning care, the nurse observes that the client washes only the right side of the face and body and leaves all the food on the left side of the meal tray untouched. Which nursing action is the priority?
options: Cue the client to attend to the left side of the body and environment, initially placing items within the client's intact visual field and gradually encouraging scanning to the left
Complete all hygiene and feeding tasks for the client to conserve the client's energy
Permanently position all personal items and food only on the client's right side
Avoid mentioning the neglect to prevent embarrassing the client
rationale: Unilateral neglect is managed by consistently cueing the client to attend to the affected (left) side and by structured scanning training, which promotes safety and supports gradual improvement in awareness while preserving as much independence as possible. Performing all care for the client (B) fosters unnecessary dependence. Permanently placing all items only on the right (C) avoids the deficit rather than addressing it and creates ongoing safety risk (e.g., missed food, injury from unseen hazards on the left). Not acknowledging the neglect (D) delays teaching the client compensatory strategies and is unsafe.
nursing_concept: Hygiene/ADL care with unilateral neglect

stem: A nurse is establishing a bowel training program for a client with chronic constipation related to a spinal cord injury. Which interventions should be included in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Schedule attempts at defecation at the same time each day, such as shortly after a meal
Increase dietary fiber intake gradually along with adequate fluid intake
Encourage an upright, seated position on a toilet or commode when possible
Administer a stimulant laxative every day as the primary long-term method
Use digital stimulation or a suppository at the scheduled time, as ordered
Restrict fluid intake to reduce the frequency of bowel movements needed
rationale: Effective bowel training uses a consistent daily schedule, ideally timed after meals to take advantage of the gastrocolic reflex (A); adequate fiber and fluid to form soft, bulky stool (B); an upright seated position that uses gravity and proper pelvic floor mechanics (C); and digital stimulation or a suppository at the scheduled time as an evacuation trigger (E). Daily stimulant laxatives as the primary long-term strategy (D) are avoided when possible because of dependency and mucosal changes with chronic use; a step-based approach starting with less invasive measures is preferred. Restricting fluids (F) worsens constipation rather than helping it.
nursing_concept: Bowel training program components

stem: The nurse assesses the heel of a client who has been immobile after a stroke. The skin is intact, but there is a localized, non-blanchable area that is purple/maroon in color, and the surrounding tissue feels boggy compared with adjacent skin. There is no open wound. Which finding should the nurse document, using current NPIAP staging terminology?
options: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Deep tissue pressure injury (suspected)
Unstageable pressure injury
rationale: A deep tissue pressure injury presents as intact or non-intact skin with a localized area of persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, and the tissue may feel boggy, mushy, or have a temperature change compared with adjacent tissue, reflecting damage to underlying soft tissue. Stage 1 (A) shows intact skin with non-blanchable erythema that is red, not purple/maroon, and without boggy texture. Stage 2 (B) requires an open wound with partial-thickness skin loss, which is not present here. Unstageable (D) requires full-thickness tissue loss obscured by slough or eschar, which does not match this intact-skin presentation.
nursing_concept: NPIAP staging — deep tissue pressure injury

stem: A client recovering from a total knee replacement is learning to ambulate with a standard four-point (non-wheeled) walker under partial weight-bearing precautions on the operative leg. Which instruction should the nurse include?
options: Move the walker forward about 6 to 8 inches, then step forward with the operative leg followed by the non-operative leg
Move the walker forward about 2 feet, then bring both legs forward together in one large step
Lean forward onto the walker's hand grips with each step to shift weight off the operative leg
Carry the walker up each stair, step by step, instead of using the stair handrails
rationale: A walker should be advanced only a short distance (about 6-8 inches) to keep it within a safe, stable base of support, with the weaker/operative leg stepping into the walker first, followed by the stronger leg. Moving the walker 2 feet at once (B) extends it beyond a safe base and increases fall risk. Leaning forward onto the hand grips (C) shifts the center of gravity forward and can cause the client to pitch forward or overload the wrists instead of bearing weight as prescribed. Walkers are not used on stairs; handrails, not the walker, should be used for stair climbing (D).
nursing_concept: Standard walker ambulation technique

stem: The nurse is using a gait (transfer) belt to assist a client with generalized weakness to transfer from the bed to a bedside chair. Which technique is correct?
options: Apply the belt snugly against the client's bare skin at the waist and grasp it with an overhand grip
Apply the belt over the client's clothing at the waist, leaving room for two fingers to fit flat underneath, and grasp it with an underhand grip
Apply the belt around the client's chest, over the axillae, for additional upper-body support
Apply the belt loosely around the client's hips and pull the client upward by the arms during the transfer
rationale: A gait belt should be applied over clothing (not bare skin, to avoid friction/shearing injury), snug enough that only two fingers fit flat underneath, and grasped with an underhand grip, which gives the nurse a secure hold without hyperextending the wrist. Placing it over the axillae/chest (C) risks rib injury and restricts breathing and is not standard placement. A loose belt at the hips with pulling on the arms (D) provides no real control and risks shoulder injury, especially in a frail client.
nursing_concept: Gait/transfer belt use

stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has been immobile for several days after spinal surgery and is using intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) sleeves for venous thromboembolism prevention. The nurse notes the client's left calf is warmer, more swollen, and more tender to palpation than the right calf. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Apply the IPC sleeve to the left leg first to help reduce the swelling
Massage the left calf firmly to improve circulation and break up any possible clot
Discontinue IPC sleeve use on the left leg, keep the client on bedrest, and notify the provider immediately
Ambulate the client in the hallway to see whether walking relieves the leg symptoms
rationale: New unilateral warmth, swelling, and tenderness are concerning for a deep vein thrombosis. The priority is to stop mechanical compression on the affected leg (to avoid dislodging a possible clot), keep the client still, and notify the provider for prompt evaluation (e.g., Doppler ultrasound). Continuing to compress or exercise the leg (A, D) or massaging it (B) could dislodge a thrombus and precipitate a pulmonary embolism.
nursing_concept: Recognizing suspected DVT in the immobile client

stem: Two nurses are preparing to logroll a client who has cervical spine precautions, repositioning the client from supine to a side-lying position while maintaining spinal alignment. Place the following actions in the correct order.
options: Place a pillow lengthwise between the client's knees and support the back with a pillow or rolled blanket
On a coordinated count, turn the client's head, shoulders, trunk, and hips simultaneously as a single unit
Explain the procedure to the client and raise the bed to a safe working height
Position one nurse at the client's head and shoulders and the other at the hips and legs, each grasping the far edge of the draw sheet
Cross the client's arms over the chest
rationale: The nurses first explain the procedure and raise the bed to a safe height, then cross the client's arms over the chest so the limbs do not catch during the turn, then each nurse positions at the head/shoulders or hips/legs and grasps the draw sheet for full-body control, then turns the client's head, shoulders, trunk, and hips together on a coordinated count to keep the spine aligned, and finally places supportive pillows to maintain the new position. Turning before both nurses are positioned, or omitting the coordinated count, risks twisting the spine and injury.
nursing_concept: Logrolling with spinal precautions

stem: A client with chronic osteoarthritis pain asks the nurse about nondrug ways to help manage pain at home. Which technique should the nurse suggest as an example of a nonpharmacological, mind-body comfort intervention?
options: Guided imagery, such as focusing on a calming mental scene paired with slow breathing
Applying a topical NSAID gel to the affected joints
Taking an extra dose of the prescribed oral analgesic before activity
Scheduling a corticosteroid joint injection with the rheumatologist
rationale: Guided imagery combined with slow breathing is a nonpharmacological, mind-body relaxation and distraction technique that can reduce the perception of pain. Topical NSAID gel (B), additional analgesic dosing (C), and a corticosteroid injection (D) are all pharmacologic/medical interventions, not nonpharmacological comfort measures, and extra analgesic dosing beyond what is prescribed (C) is also unsafe.
nursing_concept: Nonpharmacological pain management

stem: A nurse is developing a plan of care for a client with chronic pain from fibromyalgia who wants to minimize reliance on opioid medication. Which nonpharmacological interventions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Guided imagery and progressive muscle relaxation exercises
A structured, low-impact aerobic exercise program such as walking or water aerobics
Application of superficial heat (e.g., a warm pack) to tender muscle areas
Cognitive behavioral therapy to address pain-related thoughts and coping
Strict bedrest to conserve energy and minimize muscle use
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) as an adjunct for localized pain
Complete elimination of all physical activity until the pain resolves
rationale: Evidence-based nonpharmacological management of fibromyalgia includes relaxation/imagery techniques (A), graded low-impact aerobic exercise (B), superficial heat for muscle comfort (C), cognitive behavioral therapy for pain coping (D), and TENS as an adjunct (F). Strict bedrest or eliminating activity (E, G) is contraindicated; deconditioning from inactivity is associated with increased pain sensitivity and worse functional outcomes in fibromyalgia, so graded activity is recommended instead of rest.
nursing_concept: Nonpharmacological pain management in chronic pain syndromes

stem: A hospitalized client reports trouble sleeping because of frequent nighttime interruptions for vital signs, medications, and lab draws. Which nursing intervention best promotes the client's rest?
options: Cluster nursing care activities, such as vital signs, medication administration, and assessments, to minimize nighttime interruptions whenever possible
Turn on the overhead room light at each round to ensure an accurate assessment
Wake the client every 2 hours overnight to reassess pain level regardless of current comfort
Encourage the client to watch television in the room until midnight to feel more tired
rationale: Clustering care activities reduces the number of times the client is disturbed, preserving longer uninterrupted sleep periods and supporting normal sleep cycles. Bright overhead lighting (B) suppresses melatonin and disrupts circadian rhythm. Waking a client who is currently comfortable on a fixed schedule (C) causes unnecessary sleep fragmentation. Screen use close to bedtime (D) is stimulating and delays sleep onset rather than promoting it.
nursing_concept: Sleep hygiene for the hospitalized client

stem: A client newly diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea has been prescribed continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy for use during sleep. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of the therapy?
options: "I should use the CPAP machine every night, including naps, at the pressure setting that was prescribed for me."
"I only need to wear the mask on nights when I feel especially tired."
"If the mask feels uncomfortable, I should stop using the machine rather than ask about adjusting the fit."
"I don't need to clean the mask and tubing regularly, since the airflow keeps them clean."
rationale: CPAP is most effective with consistent use every time the client sleeps, including naps, at the prescribed pressure, to keep the upper airway open throughout sleep. Intermittent use (B) leaves apnea episodes unmanaged on nights the mask is skipped. Discomfort should prompt a request for mask refitting or a different interface, not discontinuation of therapy (C). Regular cleaning of the mask and tubing per manufacturer instructions is needed to prevent bacterial/mold growth and skin irritation; airflow alone does not clean the equipment (D).
nursing_concept: CPAP therapy teaching for obstructive sleep apnea

stem: The nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious, orally intubated client receiving mechanical ventilation. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Position the client supine with the head of the bed flat during oral care to prevent gagging
Suction oral secretions as needed during care, use a chlorhexidine-based oral rinse per protocol, and keep the head of the bed elevated 30-45 degrees
Use a standard toothbrush and ordinary toothpaste, and have the client rinse and spit after each brushing
Limit oral care to once every 24 hours to avoid disturbing the client's rest
rationale: An evidence-based ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle includes keeping the head of the bed elevated 30-45 degrees, suctioning oral secretions/fluid during care to prevent aspiration, and using a chlorhexidine-based oral rinse per protocol, performed more often than once daily (commonly every 2-4 hours). Flat positioning (A) increases aspiration risk. An unconscious client cannot rinse and spit (C); doing so would cause aspiration. Limiting oral care to once daily (D) is inadequate and is associated with increased VAP risk.
nursing_concept: Oral care for the ventilated client / VAP prevention

stem: The nurse is giving a complete bed bath to a client who is fully dependent for hygiene care. Place the following actions in the correct order.
options: Wash, rinse, and dry the face, neck, and ears, moving from the cleanest to the most soiled areas
Fill the basin with warm water and test the temperature before beginning
Perform hand hygiene, don gloves, and provide for privacy by closing the door or curtain
Wash, rinse, and dry the arms and hands, followed by the chest and abdomen
Change the bath water, then wash, rinse, and dry the legs and feet
Change the water again and wash the perineal area last, using a clean section of the washcloth for each area and wiping front to back
rationale: Bathing begins with hand hygiene, glove use, and ensuring privacy, followed by preparing water at a safe, comfortable temperature. Washing then proceeds from cleaner areas (face/neck/ears) to progressively less clean areas (arms/trunk, then legs/feet), changing the bath water partway through and again before perineal care, which is done last with a clean section of washcloth per area and a front-to-back wiping direction, to avoid transferring microorganisms from less clean to cleaner body areas or introducing rectal flora toward the urethra.
nursing_concept: Complete bed bath sequence

stem: A nurse is caring for a client recovering from a stroke who has been cleared by speech-language pathology for an oral diet with thickened liquids due to dysphagia. Which actions should the nurse include when assisting this client with meals? Select all that apply.
options: Position the client upright at 90 degrees, if possible, for all oral intake
Offer small bites and sips, allowing time for the client to swallow completely before the next bite
Check the client's mouth for pocketed food after each bite and at the end of the meal
Have the client tilt the head backward slightly while swallowing to ease the passage of food
Keep the client upright or in a side-lying position with the head elevated for at least 30 minutes after the meal
Mix the client's pills into a full glass of thin water to make them easier to swallow
Provide thin liquids instead of the prescribed thickened liquids if the client requests them
rationale: Safe feeding for dysphagia includes upright positioning at 90 degrees during intake (A), small bites/sips with adequate time to swallow (B), checking for pocketed food that could later be aspirated (C), and remaining upright for at least 30 minutes after eating to reduce reflux/aspiration risk (E). Tilting the head backward (D) extends the neck and opens the airway to food, increasing aspiration risk; the chin-tuck position is used instead. Giving pills in thin water (F) or substituting thin liquids for the prescribed thickened consistency (G) disregards the ordered dysphagia diet and increases aspiration risk, regardless of client preference.
nursing_concept: Dysphagia diet and safe swallowing precautions

stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a long-term indwelling urinary catheter. Which assessment finding should the nurse recognize as a sign of a possible catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) warranting provider notification, rather than an expected finding in a client with a chronic indwelling catheter?
options: Urine that appears cloudy with sediment but has no odor change, as has been typical for this client for months
New-onset fever, suprapubic tenderness, and cloudy, foul-smelling urine
A slight ammonia-like urine odor that is more noticeable after several hours without a drainage-bag change
Scant, nonpurulent pericatheter mucus at the insertion site in a client with a long-standing catheter
rationale: New fever with suprapubic tenderness and malodorous, cloudy urine represents a change from baseline along with systemic and local signs suggestive of CAUTI, which should be reported to the provider. Options A and C describe unchanged, longstanding baseline findings common in chronically catheterized clients (asymptomatic bacteriuria is frequent and is not treated unless the client is symptomatic). Option D describes a minor, nonpurulent finding without accompanying systemic or local signs of infection, which alone is not diagnostic of CAUTI.
nursing_concept: Recognizing CAUTI vs. expected chronic catheter findings

stem: A nurse is caring for a 2-year-old who insists on putting on their own shoes, becomes tearful and shouts "No, me do it!" when the parent tries to help, and resists sitting still for a diaper change. According to Erikson's theory of psychosocial development, which statement best explains this behavior?
options: The child is exhibiting stranger anxiety typical of the trust versus mistrust stage
The child is working through the developmental task of autonomy versus shame and doubt by asserting independence
The child is displaying signs of an attachment disorder that warrants an immediate referral
The child is regressing because the industry versus inferiority stage was not successfully achieved
rationale: Toddlers (roughly 1 to 3 years) are working through Erikson's autonomy versus shame and doubt stage, during which insisting on doing things independently, negativism, and brief frustration/tantrums when thwarted are expected, healthy attempts to establish self-control and independence. Trust versus mistrust (A) is the infancy stage (birth to about 18 months) centered on the caregiver relationship, not self-assertion. Labeling normal toddler independence as an attachment disorder (C) is an overreaction to developmentally expected behavior. Industry versus inferiority (D) applies to school-age children (about 6 to 12 years) mastering skills and competence, not toddlers.
nursing_concept: Erikson's psychosocial stages — toddler autonomy vs. shame and doubt

stem: At 1 minute after birth, a newborn has a heart rate of 130 beats/min, a slow and irregular respiratory effort, some flexion of the extremities, a grimace in response to suctioning, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What is this newborn's 1-minute APGAR score?
rationale: Each APGAR component is scored 0-2: heart rate >100 beats/min = 2 points; slow, irregular respirations = 1 point; some flexion of extremities (muscle tone) = 1 point; grimace/facial movement in response to stimulation (reflex irritability) = 1 point; and a pink body with blue extremities, i.e., acrocyanosis (color) = 1 point. The total is 2+1+1+1+1 = 6, not 4, 8, or 10.
nursing_concept: APGAR scoring at 1 and 5 minutes

stem: A nurse is performing an initial assessment of a full-term newborn 2 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Which findings should the nurse recognize as expected for this newborn? Select all that apply.
options: Toes fan outward and the big toe dorsiflexes when the sole of the foot is stroked (positive Babinski reflex)
Axillary temperature of 36.5°C (97.7°F)
Sustained respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min at rest
Symmetric abduction and extension of the arms in response to a sudden loud noise (positive Moro reflex)
Apical heart rate of 130 beats/min
Bluish discoloration of the hands and feet with a pink body (acrocyanosis)
Anterior fontanel that is firm, bulging, and tense while the newborn is quiet and not crying
rationale: A positive Babinski reflex (A) is a normal newborn finding that disappears by about 1 year of age. An axillary temperature of 36.5°C (B), a heart rate of 130 beats/min (E), a positive Moro reflex (D), and acrocyanosis (F) are all expected newborn findings. A sustained respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min (C) is tachypnea outside the normal newborn range of about 30-60 breaths/min at rest and should be reported, not assumed normal. A firm, bulging, tense anterior fontanel while quiet (G) is an abnormal finding suggestive of increased intracranial pressure; a normal fontanel is soft and flat (it may bulge briefly only with crying or straining).
nursing_concept: Expected newborn reflexes and vital sign ranges

stem: Two hours after a vaginal delivery, the nurse palpates a client's fundus and finds it boggy and displaced above the umbilicus toward the right side. The perineal pad is saturated with lochia rubra. What should the nurse do first?
options: Notify the primary care provider immediately
Administer intramuscular oxytocin per protocol
Massage the fundus until it becomes firm
Document the finding and reassess in 1 hour
rationale: A boggy, poorly contracted fundus signals uterine atony, the leading cause of early postpartum hemorrhage, so the nurse's immediate independent action is to massage the fundus until it firms up. Fundal displacement above the umbilicus and to one side classically indicates a full bladder pressing the uterus out of midline; if massage does not keep the fundus firm, the nurse should next have the client void or catheterize as needed, but reducing active hemorrhage risk with massage comes first. Administering oxytocin (B) may follow if massage alone is ineffective, and notifying the provider (A) or simply reassessing later (D) both delay an intervention the nurse can and should perform immediately.
nursing_concept: Postpartum fundal assessment — uterine atony and bladder distention

stem: The nurse is assessing an 78-year-old client during a routine wellness visit. Which finding should the nurse recognize as an expected, normal change of aging rather than a sign of a new acute problem?
options: Gradual, symmetric loss of hearing for high-pitched sounds that has developed slowly over several years
Sudden hearing loss in one ear that began yesterday
New-onset resting tremor with rigidity and a shuffling gait
Acute confusion and disorientation that began this morning
rationale: Gradual, bilateral high-frequency hearing loss (presbycusis) is a common, expected age-related sensory change. Sudden unilateral hearing loss (B) is an otologic emergency requiring prompt evaluation, not a normal aging change. New resting tremor with rigidity and shuffling gait (C) suggests parkinsonism, a new pathological finding, not normal aging. Acute-onset confusion (D) indicates delirium, a medical emergency that must be distinguished from the slow, gradual cognitive changes sometimes seen with normal aging.
nursing_concept: Normal changes of aging vs. pathological findings

stem: A 46-year-old client with no personal or family history of colorectal cancer and no gastrointestinal symptoms asks the nurse when routine colorectal cancer screening should begin. Which response is most accurate based on current general screening guidance for an average-risk adult?
options: "Screening is not recommended until age 65."
"Because you are over 45 and at average risk, you should begin routine colorectal cancer screening now."
"Screening is only necessary once you develop symptoms such as blood in the stool."
"You would need a first-degree relative with colon cancer before screening is recommended."
rationale: Current general guidance recommends that average-risk adults begin routine colorectal cancer screening around age 45, since the purpose of screening is to detect disease before symptoms appear. Waiting until age 65 (A) delays screening well past the recommended start. Waiting for symptoms (C) defeats the purpose of screening, which targets asymptomatic disease. A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer (D) would actually indicate a need for earlier, more frequent screening based on increased risk, not a prerequisite for screening at all.
nursing_concept: Age-appropriate cancer screening guidance

stem: A nurse is providing health education to a group of adults about routine health screening. Which statements should the nurse include as accurate general guidance? Select all that apply.
options: "Blood pressure should be checked at every routine healthcare visit, since hypertension often causes no symptoms."
"Adults at average risk should have their blood cholesterol (lipid) levels checked periodically starting in early adulthood."
"Cervical cancer screening is generally recommended for average-risk individuals with a cervix starting in their 20s, at intervals set by their provider."
"Performing skin self-checks and having any new or changing mole evaluated by a provider supports early detection of skin cancer."
"Once a person turns 40, no further cancer screening is needed for the rest of their life."
"Screening tests are only performed after a person already has symptoms of disease."
rationale: Routine blood pressure checks (A), periodic lipid screening beginning in early adulthood (B), cervical cancer screening starting in the 20s (C), and skin self-examination with prompt evaluation of concerning moles (D) are all accurate elements of general, evidence-based screening guidance for average-risk adults. Claiming that screening stops entirely at age 40 (E) is false; screening recommendations and intervals continue to be individualized throughout adulthood based on age, risk factors, and overall health status. Screening tests are, by definition, performed on asymptomatic people to detect disease early (secondary prevention), not only after symptoms appear (F).
nursing_concept: Routine health screening intervals across adulthood

stem: During a well-visit, a 15-year-old tells the nurse, "A lot of my friends vape, and I've tried it a few times because it's supposed to be safer than cigarettes." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "You're right, vaping is a much safer alternative to cigarettes, so it's not something to worry about."
"E-cigarettes still deliver nicotine and other harmful chemicals, can lead to nicotine addiction, and increase the likelihood of trying other tobacco products."
"I need to tell your parents about this right away."
"As long as you don't vape every day, occasional use isn't a health concern."
rationale: The nurse should provide accurate, nonjudgmental education: e-cigarettes are not a safe alternative — they expose users, especially adolescents with still-developing brains, to nicotine and other harmful chemicals, promote nicotine addiction, and are associated with increased likelihood of using other tobacco products. Calling vaping "much safer" (A) or dismissing occasional use as risk-free (D) reinforces a dangerous misconception. Immediately involving the parents without further discussion (C) is not the priority first response and can shut down an open conversation that supports honest disclosure and counseling.
nursing_concept: High-risk behavior counseling — adolescent vaping/tobacco use

stem: A 40-year-old client with no cardiovascular disease and a sedentary desk job asks the nurse how much physical activity is recommended to promote health. Which response reflects current general health promotion guidance for a healthy adult?
options: "Aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, along with muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days a week."
"You need to run at least 5 miles every day to see any health benefit."
"Physical activity is unnecessary as long as your diet is healthy."
"You should avoid exercise entirely until you lose weight first."
rationale: General evidence-based guidance for healthy adults recommends at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days per week, with benefits achievable through activities as simple as brisk walking. Requiring daily 5-mile runs (B) is an unrealistic and unnecessarily extreme threshold. Diet alone does not replace the cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and mental health benefits of physical activity (C). Advising a client to avoid exercise until weight loss occurs (D) is inaccurate and counterproductive, since regular activity itself supports healthy weight management.
nursing_concept: Lifestyle counseling — physical activity recommendations

stem: A nurse has just finished teaching a client how to self-administer subcutaneous insulin injections. Which action best allows the nurse to evaluate whether the teaching was effective?
options: Ask the client, "Do you understand how to give the injection?"
Ask the client to explain and demonstrate the steps of drawing up and injecting the insulin in their own words
Give the client a pamphlet about insulin administration to read at home
Document that teaching was completed and move on to the next task
rationale: The teach-back method — having the client explain and demonstrate the information in their own words and actions — is the most reliable way to confirm actual understanding and identify gaps, and it accounts for health literacy differences. A closed yes/no question like "Do you understand?" (A) is unreliable because clients often answer "yes" regardless of true comprehension. Providing written material alone (C) does not confirm understanding, particularly for clients with limited health literacy. Documenting teaching as complete without verifying comprehension (D) skips evaluation entirely.
nursing_concept: Teach-back method / evaluating learning

stem: The nurse is planning a discharge teaching session for a client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes who will be self-monitoring blood glucose at home. Place the following steps of the teaching session in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Assess the client's current knowledge, health literacy, and readiness to learn
Demonstrate the steps of blood glucose self-monitoring using the client's own equipment
Provide the information in short segments using clear, non-medical language and appropriate materials
Have the client perform a return demonstration using the teach-back method
Document the teaching provided and the client's demonstrated level of understanding
rationale: Effective client teaching begins by assessing the client's baseline knowledge, health literacy, and readiness to learn, since this determines how the content should be paced and presented. Next, the nurse delivers the information in manageable segments using plain language appropriate to the client's literacy level, followed by a hands-on demonstration of the actual skill using the client's own supplies. The client then performs a return demonstration/teach-back so the nurse can verify understanding, and finally the nurse documents the teaching provided and the client's demonstrated competence. Performing the steps out of this order — for example, demonstrating or testing understanding before assessing readiness and providing information — undermines learning and produces an inaccurate evaluation.
nursing_concept: Principles of teaching/learning — structuring a teaching session

stem: A community health nurse organizes a smoking cessation support group for clients who have already been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with the goal of slowing disease progression and preventing complications. This activity is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention
rationale: Tertiary prevention focuses on minimizing the effects and complications of an already-diagnosed disease and restoring or maintaining function, which describes this COPD support group. Primary prevention (A) aims to prevent disease before it occurs, such as encouraging people who have never smoked to remain tobacco-free. Secondary prevention (B) involves early detection of disease that is present but not yet symptomatic, such as screening tests. Quaternary prevention (D) refers to avoiding unnecessary or excessive medical intervention, which is not what is described here.
nursing_concept: Levels of prevention — primary, secondary, tertiary

stem: A home health nurse is visiting an 82-year-old client who lives alone and takes nine different prescription medications for multiple chronic conditions. The client appears unsteady when rising from a chair and reports two near-falls in the past month. Which factor should the nurse recognize as most directly increasing this client's fall risk?
options: The client's chronological age by itself
Polypharmacy combined with age-related slowing of balance, reaction time, and gait
The client's decision to continue living independently
A diet that includes high-fiber foods
rationale: Taking multiple medications (polypharmacy) combined with expected age-related changes in balance, proprioception, and reaction time is one of the strongest, most modifiable contributors to falls in older adults, and this client's near-misses and unsteadiness are consistent with that combination. Age alone (A) is not itself a risk factor to act on and reflects an ageist assumption rather than an assessable cause. Choosing to live independently (C) is not inherently a risk factor; many older adults live safely and independently with appropriate supports. A high-fiber diet (D) is a healthy habit and has no direct link to fall risk.
nursing_concept: Normal changes of aging and fall-risk assessment

stem: A 16-year-old client at a routine clinic visit describes trying out different friend groups and styles of dress, questioning what career to pursue, and feeling unsure "who I really am" some days. The parent, who is present, appears concerned and asks the nurse if this is normal. Which response reflects the nurse's correct analysis of this behavior?
options: This pattern suggests a mood disorder that requires an immediate psychiatric referral
This reflects identity versus role confusion, the expected adolescent developmental task of exploring values, roles, and relationships before forming a stable sense of self
This behavior shows the adolescent has regressed to the industry versus inferiority stage
This pattern meets the criteria for a conduct disorder
rationale: According to Erikson, adolescence centers on identity versus role confusion, during which trying on different roles, appearances, and peer groups while questioning one's future is a normal, expected developmental process rather than a pathological one. Without additional findings such as persistent sadness, loss of interest, or functional decline, labeling this a mood disorder needing urgent referral (A) is an overreaction to developmentally expected exploration. Industry versus inferiority (C) describes school-age children mastering skills and competence, which does not fit this scenario. Conduct disorder (D) requires a persistent pattern of rule-violating or aggressive behavior, which is not described here.
nursing_concept: Erikson's psychosocial stages — adolescent identity vs. role confusion

stem: An outpatient nurse is teaching a 65-year-old client with no chronic illnesses about disease-prevention strategies appropriate for their age group. Which statement by the nurse reflects accurate primary prevention guidance?
options: "You no longer need any vaccines once you reach your 60s, since your immune system is already fully primed."

"Staying current on vaccines recommended for your age group, such as annual influenza and age-appropriate pneumococcal and shingles (herpes zoster) vaccines, is an important way to prevent serious illness."
"Vaccines are only beneficial for young children and provide little benefit to adults."
"It's best to wait until you actually develop pneumonia before considering a pneumococcal vaccine."
rationale: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it occurs, and remaining current on vaccines recommended for older adults (such as influenza, pneumococcal, and shingles vaccines) reduces the risk of serious complications from preventable illness. Claiming older adults no longer need vaccines (A) is inaccurate; immune responses actually tend to wane with age, making prevention more, not less, important. Suggesting vaccines only benefit children (C) ignores well-established adult immunization guidance. Waiting until disease develops before vaccinating against it (D) confuses prevention with treatment and defeats the purpose of primary prevention.
nursing_concept: Primary prevention — adult immunization

stem: A nurse is teaching a 50-year-old client at average risk for breast cancer about routine breast health screening. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: "Routine mammography screening is recommended at intervals appropriate for your age and risk level; ask your provider what schedule is right for you."
"Report any new breast lump, skin change, nipple discharge, or persistent breast pain to your provider promptly."
"Breast self-awareness — knowing how your breasts normally look and feel — helps you notice changes to report, even though self-exam alone is not a substitute for clinical screening."
"Because you have no family history of breast cancer, you will never need a mammogram."
"A normal mammogram result means you never need to report any future breast changes again."
"A clinical breast examination by a provider may be offered as part of your routine physical exam."
"Mammography is completely painless and takes less than one minute total for both breasts combined."
rationale: Individualized mammography scheduling (A), prompt reporting of new breast changes (B), breast self-awareness as a complement to (not a replacement for) clinical screening (C), and clinical breast exams during routine visits (F) are all accurate, evidence-based teaching points for an average-risk client. Most breast cancers occur in people without a family history, so lacking one (D) does not eliminate the need for screening. A prior normal mammogram does not prevent new changes from developing, so ongoing self-awareness and reporting remain necessary (E). Mammography can involve brief discomfort or pressure for some clients, so promising it is entirely painless (G) is an inaccurate overgeneralization that could undermine trust in the teaching.
nursing_concept: Breast cancer screening guidance for average-risk adults

stem: A 17-year-old tells the school nurse, "I know texting while driving is dangerous, but everyone does it, and I only check my phone when I'm stopped at red lights." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "As long as you only check your phone while fully stopped, that's a safe habit."

"Even checking a phone at a stoplight can distract you as traffic starts moving, and any phone use while driving increases crash risk — consider keeping your phone out of reach while you drive, such as in the back seat or a glove box."
"I'm required to report this behavior to the Department of Motor Vehicles."
"You should give up your driver's license entirely until you turn 18."
rationale: The nurse should correct the misconception that checking a phone only while stopped is risk-free — attention can remain diverted as traffic resumes moving — and offer a practical, nonjudgmental strategy such as placing the phone out of reach while driving. Agreeing that stoplight phone use is safe (A) reinforces a dangerous belief. Threatening to report the teen to the DMV (C) is not within the nurse's role for this disclosure and would likely shut down future honest conversation. Demanding the teen surrender their license (D) is an extreme response disproportionate to the disclosure and is not a nursing action.
nursing_concept: High-risk behavior counseling — distracted driving

stem: A nurse is counseling a client who works rotating night shifts and reports feeling constantly fatigued and irritable. Which lifestyle recommendation by the nurse best supports healthy sleep hygiene for this client?
options: "Keep your bedroom bright and use your phone to scroll before falling asleep."
"Try to keep a consistent sleep schedule, use blackout curtains to create a dark environment for daytime sleep, and limit caffeine in the hours before your scheduled sleep time."
"Drink a cup of coffee right before your daytime sleep period to help you fall asleep faster."
"Sleep is optional as long as you maintain a balanced diet."
rationale: A consistent sleep schedule, a dark sleep environment (even during daytime hours for shift workers), and limiting caffeine before the planned sleep period are evidence-based sleep hygiene strategies that support better sleep quality and reduce fatigue. A bright bedroom and screen use before sleep (A) both interfere with the body's ability to fall and stay asleep by suppressing melatonin and increasing alertness. Caffeine shortly before sleep (C) is a stimulant and would further disrupt the ability to fall asleep. Sleep is a basic physiological need, not an optional lifestyle choice that diet can substitute for (D).
nursing_concept: Lifestyle counseling — sleep hygiene for shift workers

stem: A nurse is preparing discharge instructions for a client with limited English proficiency and low health literacy who will be managing a new colostomy at home. Which action by the nurse best supports effective learning for this client?
options: Provide written instructions only in English and have the client sign a form stating they understand
Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter, use plain non-medical language with pictures or physical demonstration, and confirm understanding using the teach-back method
Speak more loudly and slowly in English so the client can better follow along
Ask a family member who is not a trained interpreter to translate the medical instructions during teaching
rationale: Effective teaching for a client with limited English proficiency and low health literacy requires a qualified medical interpreter, plain non-medical language, visual aids or demonstration, and confirmation of understanding through teach-back, since a signature or verbal "yes" does not confirm comprehension. Providing English-only written material and requiring a signature (A) does not address the language barrier or verify understanding. Speaking loudly and slowly in English (C) does not resolve a language barrier and can feel patronizing. Relying on an untrained family member to interpret medical information (D) risks inaccurate translation and compromises the client's privacy and the accuracy of the teaching.
nursing_concept: Principles of teaching/learning — health literacy and language barriers

stem: A nurse has taught a client with diabetes mellitus about daily foot care to prevent complications. Which statement by the client indicates that the teaching has been effective?
options: "I'll soak my feet in hot water every night to keep them clean."
"I'll inspect my feet every day for cuts, redness, or blisters, and wear properly fitting closed-toe shoes to protect them."
"I can go barefoot around the house since my feet feel fine."
"I only need to check my feet if they start to hurt."
rationale: Daily foot inspection and wearing properly fitting, protective footwear are core self-care behaviors that reduce the risk of unnoticed injury, infection, and ulceration in clients with diabetes, who often have reduced peripheral sensation. Soaking feet in hot water (A) can cause burns or excessive skin drying in a client with impaired sensation and is not recommended. Going barefoot (C) increases the risk of unnoticed cuts or punctures. Waiting for pain before checking the feet (D) is unsafe because diabetic peripheral neuropathy often means injuries are not felt until they have become serious.
nursing_concept: Self-care — diabetic foot care

stem: A postpartum nurse observes a breastfeeding mother and newborn during a feeding session to evaluate technique. Which observations indicate effective breastfeeding? Select all that apply.
options: The newborn's mouth covers a large portion of the areola, not just the nipple
The newborn's lips are flanged outward around the breast
The nurse hears frequent clicking sounds as the newborn sucks
The mother reports rhythmic sucking and swallowing with occasional pauses
The newborn's chin and nose are touching the breast while the nose remains free to breathe
The mother reports persistent, sharp nipple pain that continues throughout the entire feeding
The newborn repeatedly falls asleep within the first minute at the breast and needs vigorous stimulation to continue feeding
rationale: A deep latch that covers much of the areola (A), flanged (not tucked-in) lips (B), audible rhythmic sucking and swallowing with pauses (D), and the chin and nose contacting the breast while the airway stays clear (E) are all signs of an effective latch and milk transfer. Frequent clicking sounds (C) usually indicate the newborn is losing and regaining suction, a sign of an ineffective latch. Persistent, sharp pain throughout the whole feeding (F) suggests improper latch or positioning and should be corrected, not expected. A newborn who repeatedly falls asleep almost immediately and requires vigorous stimulation to keep feeding (G) suggests ineffective transfer of milk rather than a well-fed, satisfied infant.
nursing_concept: Evaluating effective breastfeeding technique

stem: A 50-year-old client reports irregular menstrual cycles, hot flashes, and difficulty sleeping over the past year. She also shares that she has been reflecting on "what's next" for her career and relationships now that her children have moved out of the home. Which statement best reflects the nurse's analysis of this client's presentation?
options: These symptoms indicate a thyroid disorder and have no relationship to normal aging
The client is experiencing the perimenopausal transition, a normal midlife developmental change that commonly involves both physical symptoms and psychosocial reflection on roles and identity
These findings meet the criteria for a major depressive episode and require immediate psychiatric hospitalization
The client's symptoms are caused entirely by poor lifestyle choices and are completely preventable
rationale: Irregular cycles, vasomotor symptoms such as hot flashes, and sleep disruption are classic physical features of the perimenopausal transition, and many women in midlife also reassess roles, identity, and relationships as children become more independent, a developmental transition sometimes referred to as the "empty nest" period. While thyroid dysfunction can cause overlapping symptoms and may be reasonable to rule out, stating the symptoms have "no relationship" to normal aging (A) is inaccurate given how classic this presentation is for perimenopause. The scenario does not describe the persistent low mood, anhedonia, or functional impairment required to diagnose a major depressive episode, so labeling this an emergency requiring hospitalization (C) is an overreaction. Perimenopause is a physiologic, hormonally driven process, not a condition caused solely by lifestyle choices (D).
nursing_concept: Midlife developmental transitions — perimenopause

stem: A nurse is screening a young adult client during a primary care visit and asks about alcohol use patterns. Which client statements should the nurse recognize as indicating a high-risk pattern of alcohol use that warrants further assessment and brief intervention? Select all that apply.
options: "I usually have 5 or more drinks in one evening when I go out with friends, a couple times a month."
"I had a glass of wine with dinner last weekend."
"I've driven home after drinking because I felt 'fine to drive.'"
"My partner has told me I should cut back, but I don't think it's really a problem."
"I sometimes need a drink first thing in the morning just to feel normal."
"I have one beer on special occasions a few times a year."
"I've missed work because I was too hungover to go in."
rationale: A pattern of 5 or more drinks in a single evening (A) meets the definition of binge drinking; driving after drinking while believing oneself to be "fine" (C) is a dangerous high-risk behavior; being told by others to cut back while minimizing the concern (D), needing a morning drink to feel normal (E), and missing work due to drinking's after-effects (G) are all classic cues of a problematic drinking pattern that map to screening questions used to identify risky alcohol use. Occasional light drinking, such as one glass of wine with dinner (B) or a single beer a few times a year (F), reflects low-risk use and is not, by itself, a cue for concern.
nursing_concept: Screening for high-risk alcohol use

stem: A healthy, full-term newborn has just been transferred from the birthing room to the nursery for routine admission care. Place the following nursing actions in the order they should typically be performed.
options: Obtain the newborn's weight, length, and head circumference
Verify that the newborn's identification bands match the mother's and confirm other security measures
Assess the newborn's temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate
Administer prophylactic erythromycin eye ointment and the vitamin K injection
Give the newborn's first bath once the temperature has stabilized
rationale: Nursery admission begins with verifying matching identification bands and security measures to prevent infant misidentification or abduction, a priority safety step before any hands-on care. The nurse then completes a baseline physiologic assessment, including temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate, to confirm the newborn is stable before proceeding. Prophylactic medications (eye ointment and vitamin K) are administered once stability is confirmed, followed by anthropometric measurements such as weight, length, and head circumference. The first bath is performed last and only after the temperature has stabilized, because early bathing before thermoregulation is established increases the risk of cold stress and associated complications such as hypoglycemia. Performing these steps out of order — for example, bathing before confirming identity or stability — compromises both newborn safety and accurate assessment.
nursing_concept: Sequencing routine newborn nursery admission care

stem: The RN charge nurse on a medical-surgical unit is making assignments for the shift. Which client should be assigned to the licensed practical/vocational nurse (LPN/VN) rather than to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: A client who needs assistance with a bed bath and repositioning every 2 hours
A client who requires routine oral medication administration and site care for a well-healing surgical incision
A client who needs vital signs measured every 4 hours and intake and output recorded
A client who needs help ambulating to the bathroom with a gait belt
rationale: Administering routine oral medications and performing wound/incision care are within the LPN/VN scope of practice in most jurisdictions but are outside the UAP scope, which is limited to basic hygiene, activities of daily living, ambulation, and collecting (not interpreting) data such as vital signs and intake/output. The bath, vital sign collection, and ambulation assistance are all appropriate UAP tasks because they are routine, non-invasive, and do not require nursing judgment.
nursing_concept: Five Rights of Delegation — right task/right person; LPN vs. UAP scope

stem: The nurse is receiving hand-off report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client 2 days post-appendectomy who rates incisional pain as 5/10
A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease whose oxygen saturation dropped from 94% to 88% and is now audibly wheezing
A client with a new colostomy who is asking questions about pouch changes
A client with stable vital signs who is scheduled for discharge teaching this morning
rationale: Using the airway-breathing-circulation framework, a client with a falling oxygen saturation and new audible wheezing has an acute, unstable respiratory change that could progress to respiratory failure and must be assessed first. The postoperative pain (A), teaching request (C), and discharge teaching (D) all involve stable clients whose needs, while important, are not immediately life-threatening.
nursing_concept: ABC prioritization — acute/unstable vs. chronic/stable

stem: A client is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization later today. Which member of the healthcare team is responsible for obtaining the client's informed consent for the procedure?
options: The RN caring for the client on the unit
The physician or advanced practice provider performing the procedure
The unit charge nurse
The admitting clerk during registration
rationale: The provider who will perform the procedure is responsible for explaining the procedure, its risks, benefits, and alternatives, and for obtaining informed consent, because only that provider can adequately answer procedure-specific questions. The RN's role is typically to witness the client's signature (confirming the client appears competent and is signing voluntarily) and to verify that the discussion took place, not to provide the procedural information itself. The charge nurse and admitting clerk have no role in obtaining consent.
nursing_concept: Informed consent — who obtains vs. who witnesses

stem: An alert and oriented client with a written advance directive stating "do not resuscitate" develops a rapidly enlarging hematoma at a peripheral IV site with local swelling and pain, but is breathing comfortably and hemodynamically stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Withhold all further treatment because the client has a do-not-resuscitate order
Contact the ethics committee before providing any care
Treat the IV infiltration/hematoma per standard nursing care, since a DNR order applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Ask the family to decide whether treatment should be given
rationale: A do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order addresses only the withholding of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (chest compressions, defibrillation, intubation for cardiac or respiratory arrest); it does not limit routine nursing or medical care for unrelated, non-life-threatening problems. The nurse should treat the IV site complication using standard practice. Withholding all care (A), deferring to the ethics committee for a routine issue (B), or shifting the decision to family when the client is alert and has already expressed preferences via the directive (D) are all inappropriate.
nursing_concept: Advance directives — scope of a DNR order

stem: A nurse is discussing HIPAA-consistent protection of client health information with a group of newly hired staff. Which statements should the nurse include as correct? Select all that apply.
options: "You may look up a former client's chart out of personal curiosity as long as you don't share what you find."
"Discuss client information only in private areas, away from public hallways, elevators, and cafeterias."
"Log out of the electronic health record any time you step away from a workstation."
"You may text a client's diagnosis to a colleague using your personal cell phone if it's quicker than the secure system."
"Share client information with other staff only on a need-to-know basis related to that client's care."
"Shred or place in a designated bin any printed documents containing client identifiers before disposal."
rationale: Protecting confidentiality requires discussing information only in private settings (B), logging out of unattended workstations (C), sharing information only on a need-to-know basis (E), and properly destroying printed materials with identifiers (F). Accessing a chart without a care-related need, even out of curiosity and even for a former client, is a HIPAA violation regardless of whether the information is shared further (A). Texting protected health information over an unsecured personal device is also a confidentiality/security violation, even if convenient (D).
nursing_concept: HIPAA-consistent confidentiality and information security

stem: A competent adult client with end-stage cancer refuses further chemotherapy despite the oncologist's recommendation and the family's wishes that treatment continue. The nurse supports the client's decision to stop treatment. Which ethical principle is the nurse primarily upholding?
options: Beneficence
Autonomy
Justice
Nonmaleficence
rationale: Autonomy is the ethical principle that respects a competent client's right to self-determination, including the right to refuse treatment, even when others disagree with that choice. Beneficence refers to acting for the client's good, justice concerns fair distribution of resources/treatment, and nonmaleficence means avoiding harm; while these principles may be relevant to the broader situation, the nurse's action of supporting the client's own decision most directly reflects respect for autonomy.
nursing_concept: Ethical principles — autonomy vs. beneficence/nonmaleficence/justice

stem: A nurse administers a medication to the wrong client but recognizes the error immediately, and the client experiences no adverse effects. After assessing the client and notifying the provider, what should the nurse do next?
options: Complete an incident/variance report documenting the event
Document in the client's medical record that an incident report was filed
Wait to see if the client develops symptoms before reporting the error
Only inform the charge nurse verbally; no written report is needed since there was no harm
rationale: Medication errors, regardless of whether harm occurred, require completion of an incident/variance report so the event can be tracked and used for systems-level quality improvement. This report is a risk-management/quality tool and should not be referenced in the client's medical record (documenting its existence there is incorrect practice); the medical record should instead objectively describe the clinical facts, assessment, and provider notification. Reporting should never be delayed pending symptom development, and a verbal-only report to the charge nurse does not fulfill the facility's reporting requirement.
nursing_concept: Incident/variance reporting for quality improvement

stem: A hospitalized client tells the nurse, "I want to leave against medical advice. I know I'm not finished with my IV antibiotics, but I need to go home." The client is alert, oriented, and able to explain the risks of leaving early. What should the nurse do first?
options: Physically prevent the client from leaving until the provider arrives
Notify the provider and prepare the against-medical-advice discharge process while respecting the client's right to refuse further treatment
Tell the client that leaving will void their insurance coverage to discourage them from going
Call security to detain the client in the room
rationale: A competent adult client has the legal and ethical right to refuse treatment and leave the hospital, even against medical advice. The nurse's role is to notify the provider, ensure the client understands the risks (informed refusal), and complete the appropriate against-medical-advice documentation while respecting the client's autonomy. Physically restraining the client (A) or involving security to detain a competent client (D) constitutes false imprisonment, and using scare tactics such as false statements about insurance (C) is coercive and unethical.
nursing_concept: Client rights — right to refuse treatment / leaving AMA

stem: A nurse is coordinating discharge planning for an older adult client who had a stroke with residual left-sided weakness and mild dysphagia. Which interdisciplinary team referrals should the nurse anticipate as appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Physical therapy for gait training and strength
Speech-language pathology for a swallow evaluation
Occupational therapy for activities of daily living retraining
Case management/social work for discharge planning and home care needs
Respiratory therapy for routine daily assessment of an unaffected respiratory system
Registered dietitian for a modified-consistency diet plan
rationale: Physical therapy (A), occupational therapy (C), speech-language pathology for the dysphagia (B), case management/social work for discharge and home-care coordination (D), and dietary consultation for a swallow-safe diet (F) are all appropriate collaborative referrals for a stroke client with weakness and dysphagia. Routine respiratory therapy assessment (E) is not indicated because the scenario describes no respiratory impairment; adding an unnecessary consult does not reflect appropriate resource use.
nursing_concept: Interdisciplinary collaboration and referrals post-stroke

stem: The charge nurse must determine the order in which to see clients at the start of the shift. Arrange the clients from the one who should be seen first to the one who should be seen last.
options: A client 1 hour post-op from a bowel resection with stable vital signs and a patient-controlled analgesia pump infusing as ordered
A client with type 1 diabetes whose bedside glucose is 42 mg/dL and who is diaphoretic and confused
A client scheduled for discharge home this afternoon who is waiting for discharge teaching
A client 3 days post-op who reports incisional pain rated 6/10 that is unrelieved by the last dose of oral analgesic given 2 hours ago
rationale: The hypoglycemic, confused client (glucose 42 mg/dL) has an immediate physiologic and safety threat and must be seen first. Next is the client with unrelieved postoperative pain despite analgesic administration, since inadequately controlled pain needs prompt reassessment and intervention. The 1-hour postoperative client is currently stable with an active PCA managing pain, so that client can be checked next. The client awaiting discharge teaching is stable and can be seen last, as this is a non-urgent, scheduled need.
nursing_concept: Prioritization — first vs. next client, ABCs and acute vs. stable

stem: A nurse floated to a specialty unit is asked to perform a task that is outside the nurse's training and competency, despite being licensed as an RN. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse to take?
options: Perform the task since the nurse holds an active RN license
Refuse the assignment outright and leave the unit
Notify the charge nurse or supervisor of the practice limitation and request an appropriate reassignment or supervised orientation to the task
Attempt the task quietly without informing anyone, to avoid seeming incompetent
rationale: A nurse is legally and ethically responsible for practicing only within their individual competency, even when floated to an unfamiliar unit. The appropriate action is to notify the supervisor of the specific skill or knowledge gap and request reassignment to tasks within the nurse's competency or supervised guidance for the unfamiliar task. Performing an unfamiliar task independently (A, D) risks client harm and exposes the nurse to liability, while refusing the entire assignment and leaving (B) is patient abandonment; the concern should be raised through proper channels instead.
nursing_concept: Legal accountability — floating and scope of individual competency

stem: A nurse is transferring a client from the intensive care unit to a medical-surgical unit. Using a standardized hand-off communication tool, which information is most important for the nurse to include?
options: The client's insurance provider and billing information
The client's current condition, recent changes in status, active treatments, and pending follow-up needs
A complete list of every medication the client has ever received during hospitalization, regardless of relevance
The names of all staff who have cared for the client during the ICU stay
rationale: Effective hand-off communication (such as SBAR) prioritizes the client's current condition, recent significant changes, active treatments/lines/drains, and pending tasks or follow-up so the receiving nurse can safely continue care without gaps. Billing information (A) is not a clinical hand-off need, an exhaustive irrelevant medication history (C) adds noise rather than safety-relevant detail, and a roster of prior caregivers (D) does not support continuity of clinical care.
nursing_concept: Continuity of care — standardized hand-off communication

stem: A client with limited English proficiency is about to sign a surgical consent form. The surgeon's qualified medical interpreter service is unavailable, so an adult family member is translating. The nurse notices the client looks hesitant and confused while the family member answers questions directly instead of translating them for the client. What is the nurse's best action as the client's advocate?
options: Allow the family member to continue since the consent conversation is already underway
Stop the consent discussion and arrange for a qualified medical interpreter (in person, phone, or video) before proceeding
Ask the family member to leave the room and postpone the signature until a relative who speaks the client's language can come in
Proceed with the procedure since a consent form was signed
rationale: The nurse's advocacy role requires ensuring the client truly understands information before consenting; a qualified medical interpreter protects accuracy and reduces the risk that a family member unintentionally filters, summarizes, or answers for the client. Continuing with an informal interpreter who is answering instead of translating (A) risks an invalid consent, and simply substituting one untrained family interpreter for another (C) does not solve the underlying problem. A signed form does not establish valid informed consent if the client did not actually understand the information (D).
nursing_concept: Patient advocacy — ensuring understanding before consent, language access

stem: A case manager reviews the chart of a client with heart failure who has had three hospital readmissions in two months. The client lives alone, has limited health literacy, and admits to running out of furosemide between refills because "it's hard to get to the pharmacy and I lose track." Which action by the case manager will best address the primary driver of this client's repeated readmissions?
options: Schedule more frequent follow-up appointments with the cardiologist
Arrange home health nursing visits and connect the client with a medication synchronization or delivery program
Advise the client to come to the emergency department sooner if symptoms worsen
Document the readmission pattern and refer the case to the risk management department
rationale: The data point directly to a medication-access and adherence barrier, so the most effective case management action targets that root cause by arranging home health support and a medication delivery/synchronization program. More frequent cardiology visits (A) does not solve the access problem, instructing earlier emergency department use (C) is reactive rather than preventive, and a risk-management referral (D) addresses institutional liability tracking, not the client's actual unmet need.
nursing_concept: Case management — identifying and addressing root causes of readmission
